work.title: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone
work.creator: J. K. Rowling

summary: Orphan Harry learns he is a wizard, finds friends at Hogwarts, learns magic, and with Ron and Hermione stops Voldemort from seizing the Philosopher's Stone.

hunger.why: The Dursleys starve Harry, the train trolley sweets and the Hogwarts feasts delight him, and Hagrid brings cake.

thirst.why: No one seeks or lacks water.

sleepiness.why: Night-time wanderings under the cloak cost sleep, a minor note.

curiosity.why: Diagon Alley, Platform Nine and Three-Quarters, Hogwarts's moving staircases, and the Forbidden Forest are a hidden world Harry discovers chapter by chapter.

explanation-seeking.why: Harry, Ron, and Hermione puzzle out Fluffy, Nicolas Flamel, and who is after the Stone, suspecting Snape.

skill-acquisition.why: Harry learns spells and potions, takes to flying at once, and trains as Gryffindor's Seeker.

play.why: Quidditch matches, wizard chess, and Exploding Snap fill the school year.

resource-accumulation.why: Harry finds his parents' gold at Gringotts, and the Stone makes gold and the Elixir of Life.

resource-foraging.why: No one searches for scarce resources.

mental-time-travel.why: The trio plan how to get past Fluffy and the obstacles.

fear-of-predators.why: The mountain troll, the three-headed dog Fluffy, and the hooded figure drinking unicorn blood in the forest threaten the children.

fear-of-aggressors.why: Voldemort, through Quirrell, tries to kill Harry, and Malfoy and the Dursleys bully him.

fear-of-heights.why: Neville falls from his broom, and Quidditch and the jinxed broomstick play on heights.

disgust.why: Troll bogeys on the wand and Hagrid's rock cakes are minor grossness.

pain-aversion.why: Harry's scar burns near Quirrell, and he is bruised by Quidditch and the troll.

pride.why: Harry is the famous Boy Who Lived, becomes the youngest Seeker in a century, and wins the house cup.

shame.why: Harry, Hermione, and Neville lose one hundred and fifty points and are shunned by Gryffindor.

moral-pride.why: Neville stands up to his friends, and Harry risks expulsion to keep the Stone from Voldemort.

guilt.why: Harry feels responsible for losing Gryffindor's points.

warmth.why: Hagrid's affection, Mrs. Weasley's jumper, and Dumbledore's gentleness surround Harry.

moral-blame.why: Malfoy's spite, Snape's unfairness, and the Dursleys' cruelty are judged throughout.

moral-praise.why: Dumbledore awards points for Ron's courage, Hermione's logic, Harry's nerve, and Neville's bravery before the whole school.

revenge.why: Harry wants to get back at Malfoy, a schoolboy grudge.

forgiveness.why: Hermione forgives Ron's cruelty after the troll.

compassion.why: Hermione's rescue by the boys and Hagrid's care for Norbert the dragon are small kindnesses.

affiliation.why: Harry meets Ron on the train and seeks friends in a world where he had none.

friendship.why: The bond of Harry, Ron, and Hermione, sealed by the troll fight, carries the story to the final obstacles.

sadness.why: Harry sees his dead parents in the Mirror of Erised and longs for them.

humor.why: Fred and George's jokes, Ron's remarks, and the absurd Dursleys keep the tone light.

embarrassment.why: Neville's mishaps and Harry's first clumsy days among wizards are lightly embarrassing.

reasoning.why: Hermione solves Snape's potion riddle and Ron wins the chess game by logic.

coalitional-affiliation.why: Sorting into houses, Gryffindor against Slytherin, and the house cup make group identity central.

status-seeking.why: House points, Malfoy's boasting, and Quidditch glory are contests for standing.

envy.why: Dudley's and Malfoy's envy of Harry are minor.

anger.why: Harry's flashes of anger at Snape and Malfoy are brief.

hatred.why: Malfoy and Snape appear to loathe Harry, and Voldemort wants him dead.

parental-care.why: Lily's sacrifice protects Harry from Voldemort, Hagrid and Dumbledore watch over him, and Mrs. Weasley takes him in.

parental-investment.why: Hagrid and Dumbledore guide and teach Harry as surrogate parents.

familial-love.why: Harry's longing for his dead parents, the warm Weasley family, and the Dursleys' cruelty frame the story.
